title: Pinchas: a shepherd for the flock (Numbers 27:15–17)
hookLine: Moses asks for a successor so the people won't be sheep without a shepherd

lines: HIS FIRST WORDS AREN'T ABOUT HIM.
cards: A doctor's office, and the news no one wants to hear. How long? What can I do?
Is there anything else? Fair first questions. Right after the five sisters' case, God tells Moses to climb a mountain and look out at the land he will not enter, because soon he will die, like Aaron.
It's hard news after so many years of leading. And the first words out of his mouth aren't about himself at all.

teach.h: HIS FIRST WORRY: THE PEOPLE AFTER HIM.
teach.b: Moses answers, in paraphrase: let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint someone over the community, who will go out before them and come in before them, who will lead them out and bring them in, and then, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd."
No protest. No bargaining for more time, not here. His first worry is the people after him.

teach.h: GOD OF THE SPIRITS OF ALL FLESH.
teach.b: Look at the name he uses for God: the God of the spirits of all flesh. Rashi hears a request inside it. You know, Moses is saying, that every person's mind is different.
Give them a leader who can bear with each of them as they are. Moses had spent his years of leading learning exactly that.

teach.h: ONE WHO GOES OUT BEFORE THEM.
teach.b: And notice the leader he asks for: one who goes out before them and comes in before them. Not one who sends people ahead, but one who walks first.
Moses had been a shepherd before he was a prophet, tending his father-in-law's flock in the wilderness when God first called him. He knew what happens to sheep with nobody in front.

The midrash adds a human touch: Moses may have hoped one of his own sons would take over. Instead God chose Joshua, who had served Moses faithfully and stayed close to the tent for years. Moses didn't argue.
The question he asked, before anything about himself, is one that parents, teachers and founders come to face too: who comes next?

how: Moses' request for a successor is read in the portion of Pinchas in summer, and the phrase 'sheep without a shepherd' is often quoted in Jewish teaching about leadership and responsibility.

games.q: you're Moses. you've just learned you won't enter the land and will soon die. what do you say first?
o: appoint someone, so they won't be sheep without a shepherd.
let my sons lead after me.
games.why: his first words are for the people: let God appoint a leader, so the congregation won't be as sheep which have no shepherd.

practice: Think of something you do that matters to others, a job, a family role, a skill, a group you hold together, and picture who would carry it if you stepped away.
What's one thing you know that they don't yet: a recipe, where the spare key is kept, a family story? Hold that one thing gently, as something worth passing on.
